strengths: The core idea of bypassing the decode step and using undecoded generative latents (3D DiT latents, discrete audio codes) directly as privileged information is a sensible and reasonably novel take on the LUGPI paradigm, motivated cleanly via a data-processing-inequality argument.

The MESSy predictive distillation objective (auxiliary heads predicting pooled teacher modality features instead of rigid L2 embedding matching) is a well-motivated alternative to standard feature distillation, addressing a real 'capacity interference' concern in asymmetric cross-modal distillation.

Reasonably broad empirical validation: results are reported on three datasets (Imagenette2, Caltech101, ImageNet-100), with 3 runs and standard deviations, modality-ablation tables, and comparisons against KD and LUGPI baselines.
Efficiency numbers for bypassing the decoder (VRAM/time savings) support the practical motivation of the method.

The NMI-based 'emergent synesthesia' analysis and class-level qualitative breakdown (acoustically- vs geometrically-driven gains) provide some interpretability evidence that the distilled modality-specific priors are meaningfully internalized rather than a trivial label leak.
weaknesses: The 'Raw vs Latent' teacher comparison (Table 1) is potentially confounded: the raw baseline uses different downstream tokenizers (PointNet++ for point clouds, 2D conv patches for mel-spectrograms) than the latent pathway's Perceiver resamplers, so improvements could partly stem from architecture/tokenizer differences rather than purely from avoiding the decode step.

The audio generation pipeline relies on captioning the image (via Gemma3) and then synthesizing audio from the caption; despite filtering class names, captions can still leak strong class-correlated semantic cues, raising concerns about whether reported audio-modality gains reflect genuine 'physical priors' vs. leaked textual/label information via the caption bottleneck.

Extremely low unimodal-only accuracies for audio/3D (e.g., 13% audio-only on ImageNet-100) suggest the synthetic single modalities are individually weak/noisy signals, which weakens the claim that these are high-quality 'privileged information' sources rather than noisy auxiliary regularizers.

Evaluation is restricted to classification on three relatively small/simple benchmarks; no evidence is given for detection, segmentation, or larger-scale/more realistic datasets, limiting claims of general applicability to computer vision broadly.

The related-work section is very thin (essentially two paragraphs), with limited engagement with the broader cross-modal distillation, feature-based KD, and multimodal representation-learning literature beyond a handful of citations.

Key implementation details (e.g., exact 3D/audio generation quality, robustness of Perceiver resampling, sensitivity to modality dropout rate, sensitivity to K in MESSy) are deferred to supplementary material not included here, limiting the ability to fully assess technical soundness and reproducibility from the main text.

The claim of 'zero additional inference cost' for the student, while true for the discarded heads, does not constitute a smaller/cheaper student model (same ViT-B/16 backbone as teacher); the efficiency narrative conflates removing multimodal input branches with genuine model compression, which could be stated more precisely.
No statistical significance testing is reported beyond mean ± std, and comparisons (e.g., MESSy vs LUGPI margins of ~3%) are not accompanied by significance analysis given only 3 runs.

No explicit discussion of failure modes, limitations of the generative augmentation pipeline (e.g., domain gap between generated 3D/audio and real signals), or societal impact, which would strengthen the completeness of the contribution.

strengths: The paper identifies a plausible and previously underexplored inefficiency in synthetic multimodal distillation pipelines — the 'decode-encode loop' — and proposes a conceptually clean fix (using undecoded generative latents directly), supported by an information-theoretic (Data Processing Inequality) motivation.

The proposed MESSy distillation objective, which uses predictive heads rather than rigid L2 feature matching, is a reasonable and lightweight solution to the capacity interference problem often observed in cross-modal distillation, and is well-motivated conceptually.

The empirical evaluation is reasonably systematic: it includes ablations on latent vs. raw data, modality contribution analysis, comparisons to KD and LUGPI baselines, and additional qualitative/NMI-based analyses of 'synesthetic' alignment, giving a multi-faceted view of the method's behavior.
Efficiency gains from bypassing decoding (VRAM/time savings for 3D and audio generation) are clearly quantified and are a useful practical contribution independent of the accuracy gains.
weaknesses: Evaluation is restricted to three relatively small/easy classification benchmarks (Imagenette2, Caltech101, ImageNet-100); there is no evaluation on larger-scale or more diverse datasets/tasks (e.g., full ImageNet, detection/segmentation), which limits confidence that the findings generalize.

The synthetic 3D and audio modalities are themselves generated from the 2D image using off-the-shelf generative models conditioned on that same image (and, for audio, an image caption). This raises a substantial risk that the 'privileged information' is largely a re-encoding of visual content already present in the image rather than genuinely independent physical priors, undermining the paper's core narrative of injecting new cross-modal information; the isolated single-modality experiments (Table 2) only partially address this concern.

No comparison is made against simpler or stronger baselines that a critical reviewer would expect, e.g., self-distillation, ensembling, standard feature-alignment with normalized/cosine losses, or existing state-of-the-art visual-only self-supervised/multi-crop augmentation methods; without these, it is hard to know how much of the improvement is attributable specifically to the 3D/audio latents versus generic regularization/ensemble effects from a heavier multimodal teacher.

The teacher network itself is trained with an aggressive modality dropout (p=0.8) and Perceiver resamplers, and no ablation isolates whether MESSy's gains stem from the specific 'synesthesia' predictive mechanism versus simply having a stronger, more regularized multimodal teacher to distill from.

Statistical significance of the reported improvements is unclear; although 3 runs are used and standard deviations are reported, several gaps (e.g., MESSy vs. LUGPI) are within or close to one standard deviation on some datasets, making the claimed superiority less certain without significance testing.

The NMI-based 'emergent synesthesia' analysis, while intriguing, uses clustering with a somewhat arbitrary number of clusters and hand-crafted/deep feature combinations; it is not clear how robust this metric is to hyperparameter choices, and no baseline sanity checks (e.g., using a strong but unrelated feature space) are provided to confirm the metric specifically captures the intended structure rather than generic feature complexity.

The paper relies on several strong-sounding but under-substantiated architectural/naming choices (e.g., 'synesthesia,' claims about 'physical priors') that are more rhetorical framing than rigorously demonstrated properties; the biological analogy to synesthesia is not carefully justified.

Reproducibility is limited: many important experimental details (hyperparameters for teacher/student training, exact prompts for Gemma3/Audiocraft, decoding thresholds, computational budget for baselines) are deferred to supplementary material not included here, making full assessment of soundness difficult.

No error bars or discussion of variance are shown in the main qualitative Fig. 4 class-level breakdown, so it is unclear if the presented 'geometrically driven' vs. 'acoustically driven' class improvements are consistent or cherry-picked examples.

The claimed 'zero additional inference cost' benefit is somewhat overstated as a novelty, since discarding auxiliary heads at inference time is a fairly standard property of many feature-distillation approaches, not something unique to MESSy.

strengths: The core idea—bypassing the decode-encode loop by using undecoded generative latents (3D DiT latents, discrete audio codes) directly as privileged information—is a clear, well-motivated, and largely novel contribution to the LUPI/LUGPI line of work, supported by a clean information-theoretic (Data Processing Inequality) argument.

MESSy distillation is a sensible and well-motivated design: replacing rigid L2 feature matching with multilayer predictive heads addresses a real and previously under-examined problem (capacity interference) in cross-modal distillation for asymmetric student/teacher architectures.

The empirical evaluation is reasonably thorough for the claims made: three datasets, three seeds per experiment with reported variance, ablations over modality combinations (Table 2), comparisons against KD and LUGPI baselines (Table 3), and quantified efficiency gains from skipping decoders (VRAM/time savings).

The 'orthogonal modality' ablation (audio-only, 3D-only performance far below Image-only) is a good sanity check against the concern that synthetic latents merely leak label information through a generative shortcut.

The NMI alignment analysis and qualitative class-level breakdown (Fig. 3, 4) provide converging, complementary evidence for the 'synesthesia' claim rather than relying on accuracy numbers alone, which strengthens the narrative that the student internalizes genuine cross-modal structure.
weaknesses: Benchmarks are relatively small-scale and simple (Imagenette2, Caltech101, ImageNet-100); it is unclear whether the reported gains generalize to larger-scale, more realistic, or more fine-grained multimodal benchmarks or to more diverse backbones.

The 'privileged information' is itself model-generated (via Hunyuan3D-2 and Audiocraft conditioned on captions/2D queries) rather than real paired multimodal data; despite the isolated-modality ablation, there remains a risk that class-correlated biases of the generative models (e.g., caption-conditioned audio synthesis) leak into the latents in ways not fully disentangled from genuine physical priors.

The comparison against alternative feature-distillation strategies is limited to plain L2 (LUGPI) and logit KD; other established feature-matching/attention-transfer techniques (e.g., cosine similarity, attention transfer, relational/correlation distillation) are not included, which weakens the strength of the 'capacity interference' claim as the definitive explanation for MESSy's gains versus simply having a more flexible objective.

Several important implementation and validation details (full generation pipeline specifics, K-layer ablation, overlap analysis for NMI clustering, raw-augmentation baseline in the distillation table) are deferred to supplementary material not included here, making full technical assessment and reproducibility judgment difficult from the main text alone.

Absolute teacher and student accuracies remain modest (e.g., ~66-72% on Caltech101/ImageNet-100), and the paper does not discuss failure cases or limitations of the approach (e.g., when synthetic latents could be unreliable or misleading, or scalability of the offline generation cost as dataset size grows).

strengths: Identifies a concrete and practically meaningful inefficiency (the decode-encode loop) in generative multimodal augmentation pipelines, and proposes a simple, well-motivated fix (using undecoded latents directly).

Careful ablation design that isolates confounds: e.g. the Raw+Perc. baseline shows the gains from latent-based teachers are not merely due to encoder/architecture differences but the representation itself.

MESSy's predictive-head distillation objective is a sensible and well-grounded extension of asymmetric predictor approaches (BYOL/data2vec/JEPA) to the cross-modal capacity-interference problem, and the paper provides direct evidence for capacity interference via a CIFAR-100 linear-probe transfer test.
Reasonably broad empirical validation across three datasets plus a scaling experiment on full ImageNet-1K, with consistent relative trends.

Interesting quantitative (NMI alignment on hand-crafted low-level features) and qualitative (per-class accuracy) analyses that attempt to demonstrate genuine structural transfer rather than label leakage or superficial correlation, including a deliberate anti-label-leakage filtering mechanism for the audio captioning pipeline.
Reports compute/efficiency savings (VRAM, generation time) quantifying the practical benefit of bypassing decoding.
weaknesses: The information-theoretic framing (DPI, mutual information chain rule) is largely a restatement of intuitive facts (decoding cannot add information, more modalities cannot decrease mutual information) and doesn't quantitatively predict or bound the empirical gains observed; it reads more as narrative justification than rigorous theory.

The audio modality is generated through an indirect image→caption(LLM)→audio pipeline, which introduces potential noise/bias from the captioning model; while a label-leakage filter is used, the audio signal's fidelity/relevance as a 'physical prior' is not independently verified beyond classification accuracy.

Core benchmarks (Imagenette2, Caltech101, ImageNet-100) are small-to-medium scale; the single ImageNet-1K result is reported without standard deviations or ablations at that scale, limiting confidence in scalability claims.
Table 4's 'Raw teacher' ablation results are reported as approximate values without uncertainty estimates, inconsistent with the rigor applied elsewhere (3 runs with std).
Only one backbone (ViT-B/16) is evaluated for both teacher and student, leaving generality across architectures/model sizes untested.

No upper-bound comparison against a teacher trained on real (non-synthetic) paired multimodal data, so it is unclear how much of the 'multimodal synergy' gap between synthetic teacher and true multimodal supervision remains.

The gains from standard KD are notably small, raising a question about whether the baseline distillation setup was optimally tuned, which could affect the magnitude of reported improvements from MESSy relative to KD.

The conceptual novelty is somewhat incremental: using diffusion/generative latents as features rather than decoded outputs, and asymmetric predictive distillation heads, both build closely on established lines of work (latent diffusion representations, BYOL/data2vec-style predictors), and the paper's contribution is primarily in combining and applying these ideas to a new cross-modal LUPI setting rather than introducing fundamentally new techniques.

strengths: The core practical problem (avoiding costly decode steps when generating synthetic auxiliary modalities for distillation) is well-motivated and the proposed bypass (DLA) is a sensible, easily-implementable idea with clear efficiency benefits (87.7% 3D speedup, 23.8% audio VRAM savings).

The experimental protocol is reasonably thorough for the chosen scale: multiple runs with std, an ablation isolating architecture vs. representation effects (Raw+Perc.), modality-ablation studies (Image+Audio, Image+3D, Audio-only, 3D-only), and a label-leakage mitigation procedure for the audio captioning pipeline.

MESSy's predictive-head formulation is a reasonable adaptation of established self-distillation ideas (BYOL/data2vec/JEPA-style) to the cross-modal LUPI setting, and the paper provides some evidence (CIFAR-100 linear probe, NMI alignment analysis) that it mitigates capacity interference better than naive L2 matching.

The paper is clearly written, well-organized (Phases 1-3, Figure 2 pipeline diagram is helpful), and includes qualitative class-level analysis that gives some intuition for which modality helps which classes.
weaknesses: Limited methodological novelty: DLA is essentially 'use the LDM/codec latent instead of decoding,' and MESSy is largely a straightforward cross-modal extension of existing predictive self-distillation frameworks (the paper itself cites AV-data2vec as 'the closest architectural predecessor' and BYOL/data2vec/JEPA as direct precedents), so the incremental contribution over this prior art is relatively thin.

The information-theoretic argument (Eq. 1-3, DPI) is largely a restatement of a well-known, almost trivial fact (a deterministic decode-then-encode chain cannot increase mutual information) and does not by itself explain or guarantee the empirically observed gap; the real driver (decoder-injected artifacts degrading the downstream encoder) is an empirical claim that is not rigorously isolated from confounds such as encoder capacity, architecture, or training schedule differences between raw and latent pipelines.

The synthetic audio-latent pipeline is a long cascade (image → Gemma3 caption → AudioGen → intercepted codes) whose semantic content is driven primarily by a captioning LLM rather than genuine acoustic measurement; despite the WordNet filtering, indirect class-correlated descriptive cues could still leak through captions, and the paper does not rigorously quantify this risk beyond the single Audio-Only accuracy check.

Evaluation is restricted to small/medium benchmarks (Imagenette, Caltech101, ImageNet-100); the single ImageNet-1K result is reported without multiple runs, error bars, or an ablation showing how MESSy/DLA design choices hold at scale, which somewhat undercuts the 'scalability' claim.

Several key design choices (hyperparameters such as β, modality dropout rate p=0.8, number of layers K, prompt design) are only ablated in supplementary material not available here and are not well justified in the main text; the hand-crafted vs deep NMI alignment analysis and the CIFAR-100 probe (42.4% vs 48.1%) are reported as single numbers with no variance, weakening the strength of the 'capacity interference' evidence.

Comparisons are limited to KD and LUGPI as baselines; no comparison to more recent/strong cross-modal distillation methods (e.g., the cited Zhao et al. trainable-projector remedy for capacity interference) that address the same stated problem, making it hard to assess how much MESSy improves over the most relevant contemporaneous alternative.

The overall pipeline depends on several large pretrained generative models (Hunyuan3D-2, Gemma-3-12B, AudioGen-Medium) plus custom Perceiver resamplers and multi-stage training; no code/data release is mentioned, and the many moving parts raise reproducibility concerns beyond what is described in the main paper.

strengths: The core motivation is clear and well-articulated: fully decoding generative latents into raw modalities before re-encoding wastes capacity and introduces decoder artifacts, and the paper backs this intuition with a clean Data Processing Inequality argument.

The MESSy predictive-head objective is a sensible and well-grounded alternative to rigid L2 feature matching, drawing appropriately from the BYOL/data2vec/JEPA lineage, and is intuitively motivated by the 'capacity interference' problem in asymmetric cross-modal distillation.

Experimental coverage is unusually thorough for this class of paper: teacher-level ablations isolating latent-vs-raw and architecture-vs-representation effects (Raw+Perc.), per-modality contribution analysis, comparisons against KD and LUGPI, a CIFAR-100 linear-probe test targeting capacity interference specifically, NMI-based alignment analysis for both low-level (HC) and semantic (Deep) modality spaces, qualitative class-level breakdowns, and a scalability check on full ImageNet-1K.
Practical efficiency claims (87.7% reduction in 3D generation time, ~24% audio VRAM savings) are concretely quantified, supporting the applied value of bypassing the decode step.

The label-leakage mitigation for the audio-caption pipeline (withholding class names, WordNet-synonym filtering, and reporting audio-only accuracy far below the image-only baseline) is a thoughtful methodological safeguard that strengthens the credibility of the modality contribution results.
weaknesses: The evaluation is confined to relatively small/easy benchmarks (Imagenette, Caltech101, ImageNet-100), and the single ImageNet-1K run is reported without repeated trials or variance, weakening confidence that the observed trends generalize to large-scale, harder settings; absolute Image-Only accuracy on ImageNet-1K (64.17%) seems low for ViT-B/16, suggesting the baseline training recipe may be relatively weak, which could inflate the reported relative gains from the multimodal augmentation.

Both auxiliary modalities are themselves hallucinated from the same RGB image (3D via image-conditioned diffusion, audio via an LLM caption of the image followed by text-to-audio generation), so the 'physical priors' the student learns are generative-model inferences rather than independent ground-truth measurements; this undercuts the strength of the 'unimodal students internalize modalities they never observed' framing, and the paper's brief acknowledgment of this in the conclusion could be developed into a more substantive limitation discussion.

The emergent-synesthesia NMI analysis clusters against features (HC/Deep) derived from the same generative teacher pipeline the student was distilled from, raising a partial circularity concern — the alignment metric is not fully independent of the training signal it is meant to validate.

It is unclear how much of the teacher's/student's improvement stems from genuinely orthogonal cross-modal information versus simply increased effective model capacity/regularization from additional tokens and heads; while Raw+Perc. partially addresses the architecture confound, no ablation isolates capacity effects for the MESSy student itself (e.g., a purely visual student with equivalent extra heads/parameters).

No results are shown on alternative backbones (e.g., CNNs or larger ViTs) or with stronger/more standard unimodal augmentation baselines, so it's unclear whether the gains persist against more competitive image-only training recipes.
Qualitative class-level analysis (Fig. 7) is presented via a small number of hand-picked examples, which is useful for illustration but not strong quantitative evidence on its own.
